subject: French Revolution
overview: Between 1789 and 1799, France tore down a monarchy that had ruled for centuries. Commoners, lawyers, Parisian crowds and rebel nobles faced the king, the old aristocracy, the Church and the monarchies of Europe, and the country went from street uprisings to a republic, a war across Europe and a period of mass executions. It ended in November 1799, when General Napoleon Bonaparte seized power in a coup and set up a government he controlled.

key_moments.title: From a tennis court to the Bastille
key_moments.text: Louis XVI had called the **Estates-General** to fix the crown's debts, but the commoners' deputies declared themselves a **National Assembly**. Locked out of their usual hall, they gathered in a nearby indoor tennis court on 20 June and swore the **Tennis Court Oath**: they would not split up until France had a constitution. On **14 July**, Parisian crowds hunting for gunpowder stormed the **Bastille**, a royal fortress-prison that stood for the king's arbitrary power. The prize turned out to be small: only **seven prisoners** were inside, and the most notorious of all, the **Marquis de Sade**, had been moved out days earlier.
claims: The deputies of the Third Estate swore the Tennis Court Oath on 20 June 1789.
A Parisian crowd stormed the Bastille on 14 July 1789.
The Bastille held seven prisoners when it was stormed.
The Marquis de Sade was transferred out of the Bastille in early July 1789, shortly before it was stormed.

key_moments.title: Privileges abolished, rights declared
key_moments.text: On the night of **4 August**, deputies in the Assembly gave up the feudal privileges of nobles and clergy one after another. Weeks later, on **26 August**, they adopted the **Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen**, which stated that men are born free and equal in rights and that sovereignty belongs to the nation. The **Marquis de Lafayette**, a veteran of the American war, helped draft it in consultation with **Thomas Jefferson**. Not everyone thought it went far enough: in 1791 the playwright **Olympe de Gouges** answered with a Declaration of the Rights of Woman, and in 1793 she was guillotined.
claims: The National Constituent Assembly abolished feudal privileges on the night of 4 August 1789.
The Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen was adopted on 26 August 1789.
Lafayette drafted the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen in consultation with Thomas Jefferson.
Olympe de Gouges published the Declaration of the Rights of Woman in 1791 and was guillotined in 1793.

key_moments.title: The monarchy falls, the king dies
key_moments.text: With France at war with **Austria** and Prussia, armed Parisians and National Guards attacked the **Tuileries Palace** on **10 August 1792**, and the king was suspended. In September the new **National Convention** abolished the monarchy and declared **France a republic**. Louis XVI, now called plain "Louis Capet", was tried by the Convention and **guillotined on 21 January 1793**. The square where he died was then the Place de la Révolution; today it is the **Place de la Concorde**, the square of harmony.
claims: Insurgents attacked the Tuileries Palace in Paris on 10 August 1792.
The National Convention abolished the French monarchy in September 1792.
Louis XVI was executed by guillotine on 21 January 1793.
Louis XVI was executed on the Place de la Révolution, now called the Place de la Concorde.

key_moments.title: The Terror and its end
key_moments.text: Facing foreign war, revolts at home and food shortages, the **Committee of Public Safety**, in which **Maximilien Robespierre** was the best-known voice, ruled through emergency measures known as the **Reign of Terror**. By common estimates around **17,000 people** were officially sentenced to death, and thousands more died in prison or were killed without trial; historians still debate how far the Terror was driven by the crisis and how far by ideology. On **27 July 1794 (9 Thermidor)** the Convention turned on Robespierre, and he was guillotined the next day. Only three years earlier, Robespierre had argued in the Assembly for **abolishing the death penalty**.
claims: The Committee of Public Safety led the French government during the Reign of Terror.
An estimated 17,000 people were officially executed during the Reign of Terror.
Robespierre was arrested on 9 Thermidor, 27 July 1794, and executed on 28 July 1794.
Robespierre spoke in favour of abolishing the death penalty in 1791.

deep_facts.text: Joseph-Ignace Guillotin, the doctor whose name became a byword for execution, was personally against the death penalty. What he proposed in 1789 was narrower: as long as France kept executing people, every condemned person, noble or commoner, should die by the same quick mechanical method rather than by hanging, the wheel or a botched sword stroke. He did not build the machine; the surgeon Antoine Louis designed it, and for a while it was nicknamed the "Louisette". The name that stuck embarrassed Guillotin's family, who later asked the government to rename the device and, when refused, changed their own surname instead. A popular story has Guillotin dying under his own machine, but he died of natural causes in 1814.
claims: Joseph-Ignace Guillotin opposed the death penalty.
Joseph-Ignace Guillotin proposed in 1789 that all executions in France use a single painless mechanical method.
The surgeon Antoine Louis designed the guillotine, which was at first nicknamed the Louisette.
Joseph-Ignace Guillotin died of natural causes in 1814, not by the guillotine.

deep_facts.text: The revolutionaries tried to restart time itself. Under the French Republican calendar, Year I began with the founding of the Republic in September 1792, and the poet Fabre d'Églantine gave the months names drawn from the weather and the farm year: Brumaire for fog, Germinal for sprouting seeds, Thermidor for summer heat. Each day lost its Catholic saint and was instead named after a plant, animal or tool, so the calendar had days for the turnip, the donkey and the wheelbarrow. Fabre d'Églantine did not see much of his calendar in use: he was guillotined in April 1794, a few months before the month he had named Thermidor brought down Robespierre.
claims: The French Republican calendar counted Year I from the founding of the Republic in September 1792.
Fabre d'Églantine named the months of the French Republican calendar after weather and seasonal farm life.
In the French Republican calendar, each day was named after a plant, animal, mineral or tool instead of a saint.
Fabre d'Églantine was guillotined in April 1794.

deep_facts.text: Antoine Lavoisier, the chemist who named oxygen and hydrogen and helped turn chemistry into a science of exact measurement, went to the guillotine on 8 May 1794. He was not executed for his science but for his side job: he was a shareholder in the Ferme générale, the hated private company that collected royal taxes, and the tax farmers were tried and condemned as a group. The judge is often quoted as saying "The Republic has no need of scientists", but the line is probably apocryphal. The mathematician Joseph-Louis Lagrange's reaction is better attested: it took only a moment to cut off that head, he said, and a hundred years might not produce another like it.
claims: Antoine Lavoisier was guillotined in Paris on 8 May 1794.
Antoine Lavoisier was executed as a member of the Ferme générale, the tax-collecting company.
The remark that the Republic has no need of scientists, attributed to Lavoisier's judge, is probably apocryphal.
Joseph-Louis Lagrange remarked that it took a moment to cut off Lavoisier's head but a century might not produce another like it.

connections.name: Louis XVI
connections.connection: The king whose debts set it off; deposed in 1792 and guillotined in January 1793.

connections.name: Maximilien Robespierre
connections.connection: Leading Jacobin on the Committee of Public Safety during the Terror, guillotined after 9 Thermidor in 1794.

connections.name: Napoleon
connections.connection: A revolutionary general who ended the Revolution by seizing power in the 1799 coup of 18 Brumaire.

connections.name: Storming of the Bastille
connections.connection: The 14 July 1789 attack on the Paris fortress-prison that became the Revolution's symbol and France's national day.

connections.name: French Revolutionary Wars
connections.connection: The wars against Austria, Prussia, Britain and others that began in 1792 and pushed the Revolution toward radicalism.

connections.name: Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen
connections.connection: Its founding statement of rights, adopted by the Assembly on 26 August 1789.

connections.name: Coup of 18 Brumaire
connections.connection: The November 1799 coup that overthrew the Directory and brought Napoleon to power as First Consul.

connections.name: Marie Antoinette
connections.connection: The queen, a target of revolutionary hatred, guillotined in October 1793.

connections.name: Georges Danton
connections.connection: Revolutionary leader and first president of the Committee of Public Safety, guillotined in April 1794 after urging moderation.

connections.name: Gilbert du Motier, Marquis de Lafayette
connections.connection: Commanded the Paris National Guard from 1789 and helped draft the Declaration of the Rights of Man.

connections.name: American Revolution
connections.connection: France's costly support for the American rebels deepened the debt crisis that led to the Estates-General of 1789.

connections.name: Haitian Revolution
connections.connection: The slave uprising in French Saint-Domingue that began in 1791, after which the Convention abolished slavery in 1794.
